title: Malignant transformation of pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma and differential diagnosis: case report
case_prompt:
A 19-year-old Japanese woman presented with left temporal headache. Brain MRI revealed a well-defined, heterogeneously contrast-enhancing 10 mm lesion in the left temporal lobe with high T2 signal. She underwent left frontotemporal craniotomy and gross total resection. Histology showed an astrocytic tumor with fewer than 1 mitosis per 10 high-power fields, and the initial diagnosis was low-grade glioma. She was followed without adjuvant therapy and had no evidence of recurrence for 3 years, then declined further examinations.

Twelve years after the initial surgery, she returned with left temporal headache, diplopia, and tinnitus. MRI demonstrated a local recurrence around the surgical cavity measuring approximately 42 × 45 × 47 mm with prominent perifocal edema. At second surgery the tumor was highly vascular with dural feeders and was weakly positive on 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic diagnosis. H&E staining showed an astrocytic neoplasm with necrosis, microvascular proliferation, infiltration, and five mitoses per 10 high-power fields; eosinophilic granular bodies were absent. Immunohistochemical studies were positive for Olig2, retained INI1 and ATRX, approximately 21% of cells were Ki-67 positive, and IDH1-R132H was negative. Retrospective review of the first specimen revealed spindle-shaped cells with nuclear pleomorphism and eosinophilic granular bodies. Both specimens lacked reticulin fibers and CD34 expression.

Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification and pyrosequencing on both resections detected a BRAF V600E mutation (mutant allele frequencies 16% initially and 49% at recurrence). The initial tumor had intact 1p/19q and CDKN2A, whereas the recurrent tumor showed 19q deletion and CDKN2A homozygous deletion. No mutations were found in IDH1/2, H3F3A, HIST1H3B, TERT promoter, or FGFR1.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. APXA was considered because of recurrence after PXA resection and increased mitotic activity but excluded by the absence of eosinophilic granular bodies — “As recurrence happened after the PXA resection, APXA was expected due to poorer histological findings; however, the tumor had no characteristic feature of PXA such as EGB, leading to a diagnosis as GBM by histological classification because of nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, a diffuse growth pattern, microvascular proliferation and necrosis.”
2. Glioblastoma was favored on histology since the recurrent tumor displayed nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, a diffuse growth pattern, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis — “leading to a diagnosis as GBM by histological classification because of nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, a diffuse growth pattern, microvascular proliferation and necrosis.”
3. A PXA-derived origin was supported by the shared BRAF V600E mutation in both resections despite absent PXA-like histology at recurrence — “the tumor origin and BRAFV600E mutations were shared in both resections suggest a PXA-derived pathology but PXA-like histology was absent.”
4. Epithelioid GBM was considered given its high rate of BRAF V600E mutations but excluded because neither specimen showed epithelioid histopathology — “Although molecular findings showed overlap with E-GBM, neither resection had a histopathology definitive for diagnosis.”
5. The molecular profile of high BRAF V600E mutant allele frequency and absent TERT promoter mutation was more consistent with APXA than with classic GBM — “From the point of molecular findings, as BRAF V600E mutation was found in 49% and TERT promotor mutations 0% of cells in the second specimen, it was consistent with APXA rather than classic GBM.”
